dossier.summary: The study provides a useful analytical account of bias in graph-agnostic regression and reports large improvements from pooling experiments with different treatment proportions. Most main simulation table values can be traced to archived arrays, and the paper acknowledges nonmonotone gains, residual bias and limits on temporal generalization. However, historical graph/feature alignment and dynamic-graph errors weaken the empirical interpretation, and unfinished zero rows materially distort the dynamic unit-level error summaries. Several controls and supplementary results lack matching delivered artifacts, while the maintained runner's corrections have not been used to reproduce the published tables. The evidence supports pooling in the studied settings more strongly than a broad recommendation to combine pooling with clustering.

claims.quote: Beyond operational benefits, we show that regression-based estimators trained on merged data achieve substantial bias reduction, even under simple randomization schemes and regression models.
scope_words: even under simple randomization schemes and regression models

claims.quote: Our closed-form analysis shows that, under regular general linear interference, bias dominates the error of the linear regression estimator.
This perspective also explains the synergy with cluster-level randomization observed in our simulations.
Across the studied interference settings, the benefits extend to lightweight GNN estimators, providing a practical way to improve counterfactual prediction using existing ramp-up data.
Merging stages with different treatment proportions reduces this bias by increasing exposure variation.

Since ramp-up is already standard practice on many online platforms, this methodology requires no additional experimentation cost and can be deployed as a plug-and-play improvement for GATE estimation under network interference.

issues.quote: Together, the experiments support combining cluster-level randomization with at least two stages having distinct treatment proportions when training a regression-based GATE estimator.
issues.why: The practical recommendation should identify observed exceptions: Table 4 at t=3 has cluster MSE 0.017 versus unit MSE 0.010, and Table 6's initial-stage pair at c_t=0.10 has 0.822 versus 0.272. These reversals limit when clustering is beneficial, while leaving the observed synergy in other settings intact.

issues.quote: Bias and standard deviation (Std) are estimated from 100 Monte Carlo repetitions.
issues.why: The archived arrays supplying Tables 1 and 3–9 have 1,000 rows, and the notebooks set repeat_num = 1000; their full-array summaries yield the reported values. The stated repetition count therefore does not describe the delivered numerical evidence.

Lemma C.1 assigns O(1/n) variance to the unnormalized quadratic form (z−w1)^T Bz. Its proof bounds the corresponding sums at O(n); the O(1/n) rate applies after the estimator's squared normalization of order n^−2, so the lemma and its use in Equation (82) need that normalization restored.

Expanding the comparison in Equation (73) gives the linear coefficient −(T−1)C1² + 2TC1C2 − T(T+1)C2; Equation (23) instead negates the middle term. For c1=0.1, c2=0.5 and x=0.9, dispersion rises from 0.190476 to 0.426667, but the printed polynomial is negative and incorrectly rejects this beneficial stage.

issues.quote: Extensive simulations across challenging scenarios confirm that our methodology significantly improves the accuracy of regression-based estimators.
issues.why: Tables report standard deviations of GATE estimates, but no test or interval for between-design accuracy differences. Large improvements are visible, but the word 'significantly' is not backed by a reported significance analysis.

issues.quote: Our theoretical analysis starts with a simple network-agnostic linear regression estimator under general linear interference.
issues.why: The linear comparator uses only intercept and treatment; an exposure-adjusted regression using the available network is absent, even for the linear-in-means setting. Section 3 explicitly calls the comparator deliberately misspecified, so this limits the practical estimator comparison rather than invalidating the stated analysis.

presentation.why: Figure 1's tick labels and dual-axis labels are extremely small at printed size; the curves are visible, but the scales are difficult to read. Figure 2 on page 8 and the ten panels of Figure 3 on page 9 have similarly tiny labels.
Tables 3–9 and 14 compress two six-metric panels into one text-width table, with very small type and tight row spacing. The printed numbers require magnification to compare comfortably.
The square-root comparison paragraph ends with the unfinished word 'while'; the next paragraph starts a new summary without completing the contrast.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: We train the GNN with Adam~\cite{kingma2014adam} to minimize MSE, using only treatment $z_i$ and degree $\deg_i$ as initial node features.
paper_mismatches.why: Features and outcome rows iterate NetworkX insertion order, while the graph is converted by dgl.from_networkx at line 114, which relabels nodes in sorted order. The delivered edge list starts with IDs 23, 1, 63, so these orders differ; graph messages consequently connect the wrong feature rows, affecting the intended network-aware estimator (also documented in docs/migration.md).

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: which randomly chooses exactly $d$ units from a population of n units to receive treatment.
paper_mismatches.why: Assignments use IDs range(num_nodes), although the delivered graph has IDs 1..num_nodes: ID 0 is ignored and the last real node is never treated. This is not uniform complete randomization over the paper's population.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: We also compare temporally independent experiments with staggered rollout
paper_mismatches.why: A new rollout_index is drawn per merged group, outside the inner loop over stage proportions at line 17103. All stages within that group reuse the vector, hence remain nested rather than temporally independent; the analogous Bernoulli notebooks do the same.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: The second combines each $c_t$ with an initial stage that treats exactly one unit or cluster, approximating a zero-treatment baseline.
paper_mismatches.why: For the initial p=0 stage, rollout_index < quantile(rollout_index,0) selects no clusters. These delivered Table 1(b) cluster results therefore use exact global control, whereas the manuscript describes one treated cluster.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Bias and standard deviation (Std) are estimated from 100 Monte Carlo repetitions.
paper_mismatches.why: The producing loop sets repeat_num = 1000, and the delivered 1000-by-5 arrays reproduce the table summaries over all rows. The maintained 100-repetition preset is a different implementation and is not the source of these values.

dgl_G is overwritten while preparing each stage and is left at the final graph, then reused for every training stage. Earlier outcomes and degree features are trained against the wrong adjacency; evaluation also uses the first selected stage's degree feature at line 43722 with that final graph.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: we preserve the clustering of the original topology $\mathcal{G}$ to implement the staggered rollout design
paper_mismatches.why: The evolved graphs are rebuilt from arrays at line 191 and receive new zero-based row labels, but cluster treatment assignments still use original node IDs. Without translating those IDs back to row positions, the communities applied to the evolving graph are not the original communities.

The delivered repeat notebooks and Repeat_Rollout_CR_* arrays implement one-hop linear-in-means outcomes, not the 2-hop control in Table 2; their values are different (unit t=5 MSE about 0.994 versus the table's 2.214). No corresponding 2-hop repeat artifact is delivered, preventing verification of the main sample-size control.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: the results demonstrate that our methodology remains effective.
paper_mismatches.why: The supplementary MIT8 graph and numerical result artifacts are absent; Cornell5 is delivered instead. This omission is acknowledged by the repository, but Table 14 cannot be traced to delivered data.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: We report its performance on two settings: multiplicative interference in Table~\ref{table:lagrange_multi} and square-root interference in Table~\ref{table:lagrange_sqrt}.
paper_mismatches.why: The repository acknowledges no complete Lagrange, MII or Hájek implementation. No matching result artifacts for Tables 11–13 were found in the delivered arrays or notebooks.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: The detailed results are reported in Table~\ref{table:lr}.
paper_mismatches.why: The maintained runner implements OLS, but the delivered historical arrays contain no matching five-stage OLS results for Table 10. The repository explicitly disclaims numerical reproduction of published tables after its corrections.

evaluation_errors.why: The saved Dynamic_CR_unit.pkl has 1,000 preallocated rows, with rows 995–999 still entirely zero; Table 7's unit-level entries equal summaries including these placeholders. Restricting to the 995 nonzero completed rows changes t=5 MSE from 0.02432156 to 0.00434328 and Std from 0.14918854 to 0.05545255; pooling still improves over one stage, but the reported error decomposition is substantially distorted.

problems.why: README.md lines 100–102 and docs/migration.md distinguish the corrected runner from the historical table arrays; the supplied validation report covers bounded engineering checks, not a complete paper replication.
notebooks/legacy/incre_2hop_CR_unit.ipynb line 196 loads A_2hop.pkl, which is not delivered. Its matrix-computation alternative is commented out.
notebooks/legacy/2hop_CR_unit.ipynb line 66 invokes node_connects_cluster before its definition at line 78 in the same cell; a fresh top-to-bottom execution needs repair.
table_output.py selects two result paths and the reference GATE manually; there is no delivered end-to-end mapping that regenerates all 14 paper tables and the exposure figures.
pyproject.toml specifies dependency lower bounds; docs/experiments.md supplies tested versions for the corrected runner, but the exact historical environment behind the table arrays is not frozen.
